cards.title: What statewide ADU laws did elsewhere
cards.text: Eight states with statewide ADU laws were measured. At a typical place with the law in force 4 or more years, their levels range from Rhode Island to California (permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year). The central scenario sits near the typical state; the lower and upper scenarios are the 10th and 90th percentiles of this spread.
cards.table_units: permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year, typical place, law in force 4+ years

cards.title: California's counts, corrected for multifamily lots
cards.text: California 2023–2025: 87,303 ADU units reported, 81,368 after the cap of 2 ADUs per parcel and the multifamily-lot rule. California is used for the shape of the response and stays in the common level because it predicts the other states better; Wisconsin's numbers are never a ratio of California's.

cards.title: Cities like Madison after a statewide law
cards.text: Nine Washington and Oregon cities similar to Madison in size and home values ran at 0.45, 0.54 and 0.60 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year in years 1–3 after their statewide law, a little over half the central scenario's statewide rate (0.77, 0.95, 0.99). Madison alone follows this observed path in every scenario; every other place follows the statewide estimate. This choice is being reviewed.

cards.title: Wisconsin today: measured permits
cards.text: Observed: Madison issued 40 second-home permits on single-family lots in 2022–2025 (0.19 per 1,000 single-family homes per year). Calculated, not observed: under current law the model expects 0.07 per 1,000 per year statewide in 2027–2031; there is no statewide ADU series. Most places have no record-level permit data, so their rates come from their rules group.

cards.title: Local ADU rules coded so far
cards.text: The largest jurisdictions' ADU rules were coded from their ordinances, with section and retrieval date for each provision. Every other place is treated as restricted.

cards.title: Places with uncoded rules behave like restricted places
cards.text: 1,882 of 1,925 areas (69% of single-family homes) have no coded rules. They get the restricted-group rate. If they behaved like prohibited places instead, the baseline would be 418 permits over 2027–2031 instead of 605.
cards.challenge: Is a rural town under county zoning really like a city with restricted ADU rules?

cards.title: Wisconsin will respond like the statewide-law states
cards.text: No Midwest state has post-law data yet. The model assumes Wisconsin's places respond like comparable places in the eight states, after adjusting for home value, income and size within each state.
cards.challenge: Iowa's first full year (2026) will be the first Midwest test.

cards.title: The law takes effect on 1 January 2027 and ramps up
cards.text: Stylized start date. In years 1–3 the addition reaches 0.63, 0.80, 0.82 of its year-4 size (central). Without the ramp, the central would be 10,268 permits instead of 8,757.
cards.challenge: A real bill would have its own effective date and local compliance deadline.

cards.title: With the law, every place reaches at least a minimum rate set from Madison
cards.text: With the law, every area's rate is at least 0.2345 permits per 1,000 single-family homes per year: Madison's 2022–2025 rate (40 permits ÷ 213.168 thousand home-years = 0.1876) divided by 0.8.

cards.title: ADUs built with a new house on a vacant lot do not count
cards.text: In 17 cities split by demolition records, vacant-lot new-house ADUs were a median 4.9% of ADUs, so every non-California series is multiplied by 0.951.

cards.title: Rural home values include acreage
cards.text: Rural areas get 3,801 of the 8,757 central permits (43%) with 710,070 of the 1,839,569 single-family homes (39%), partly because rural median home values include land. Holding rural places and small communities at the minimum rate set from Madison (0.2345) gives 4,765.
cards.challenge: Septic limits and lower demand could make rural uptake lower than this.
